claim: Alu elements account for almost 1.2 million copies in the human genome.
source: The primate-specific Alu elements are the second most prevalent class with almost 1.2 million copies, and thousands of them can be spliced to create Alu-exons (Lev-Maor et al., 2003; Sorek et al., 2004; Zarnack et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Thousands of Alu elements can be spliced to create Alu-exons.
source: The primate-specific Alu elements are the second most prevalent class with almost 1.2 million copies, and thousands of them can be spliced to create Alu-exons (Lev-Maor et al., 2003; Sorek et al., 2004; Zarnack et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated directly with supporting citations from previous studies.

claim: Only few Alu-exons encode for novel protein isoforms.
source: Only few Alu-exons encode for novel protein isoforms (Lin et al., 2016), and for several, the evolutionary history of their exonisation has been described (Krull et al., 2005; Moller-Krull et al., 2008; Singer et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated directly with a supporting citation.

claim: As few as three single nucleotide mutations from the Alu consensus sequence are sufficient to create cryptic 5' and 3' splice sites.
source: Alu elements are particularly prone to exonisation because as few as three single nucleotide mutations from the Alu consensus sequence are sufficient to create cryptic 5' and 3' splice sites (Lev-Maor et al., 2003; Sorek et al., 2004), and the left-arm Alu sequence contains a CUAUU sequence that can serve as branchpoint (Mercer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated directly with supporting citations.

claim: The left-arm Alu sequence contains a CUAUU sequence that can serve as branchpoint.
source: Alu elements are particularly prone to exonisation because as few as three single nucleotide mutations from the Alu consensus sequence are sufficient to create cryptic 5' and 3' splice sites (Lev-Maor et al., 2003; Sorek et al., 2004), and the left-arm Alu sequence contains a CUAUU sequence that can serve as branchpoint (Mercer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated directly with a supporting citation.

claim: Annotated Alu-exons are usually alternatively spliced and show low inclusion levels.
source: Annotated Alu-exons are usually alternatively spliced and show low inclusion levels (Sorek et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated directly with a supporting citation.

claim: Alu-exons often contain detrimental sequences that can lead to the production of misfolded or dominant negative protein variants.
source: Like other types of cryptic exons, Alu-exons often contain detrimental sequences that can lead to the production of misfolded or dominant negative protein variants and are therefore associated with many human diseases (Kaneko et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated directly with a supporting citation.

claim: Alu-exons are associated with many human diseases.
source: Like other types of cryptic exons, Alu-exons often contain detrimental sequences that can lead to the production of misfolded or dominant negative protein variants and are therefore associated with many human diseases (Kaneko et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated directly with a supporting citation.

claim: Virtually all human genes contain an Alu element in at least one intron.
source: Virtually, all human genes contain an Alu element in at least one intron.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction.

claim: Alu elements require a polyA-tail for their retrotransposition.
source: Alu elements require a polyA-tail for their retrotransposition (Doucet et al., 2015), and therefore, when they insert into other genes in an antisense orientation, they start with a polyuridine tract (U-tract).
evidence: This is stated directly with a supporting citation.

claim: When Alu elements insert into other genes in an antisense orientation, they start with a polyuridine tract (U-tract).
source: Alu elements require a polyA-tail for their retrotransposition (Doucet et al., 2015), and therefore, when they insert into other genes in an antisense orientation, they start with a polyuridine tract (U-tract).
evidence: This is stated directly as a logical consequence of the polyA-tail requirement.

claim: Antisense Alu elements often contain cryptic splice sites.
source: Moreover, these antisense Alu elements often contain cryptic splice sites (Lev-Maor et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated directly with a supporting citation.

claim: hnRNPC binds U-tracts in vivo to block recruitment of U2AF2.
source: While U-tracts can allow 3' splice site recognition in vitro (Bouck et al., 1998), we previously showed that the RNA-binding protein heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein C1/C2 (hnRNPC) binds these U-tracts in vivo to block recruitment of the spliceosomal factor U2 auxiliary factor 65 kDa subunit (U2AF2, also U2AF65).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the authors' previous work.

claim: Depletion experiments for TDP43, TIA, HuR, PTB and hnRNPA1 did not show increased Alu-exon inclusion in their absence.
source: Yet, depletion experiments for TDP43, TIA, HuR, PTB and hnRNPA1 did not show increased Alu-exon inclusion in their absence (Zarnack et al., 2013; Kelley et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated directly with supporting citations.

claim: The U-tract:hnRNPC interaction is crucial to prevent the splicing machinery from accessing cryptic splice sites at Alu-exons.
source: Thus, the U-tract:hnRNPC interaction is crucial to prevent the splicing machinery from accessing cryptic splice sites at Alu-exons.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the depletion experiments.

claim: Previous study of hnRNPC depletion uncovered exonisation of more than 1900 Alu elements.
source: Our previous study of hnRNPC depletion uncovered exonisation of more than 1900 Alu elements (Zarnack et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated directly with a supporting citation.

claim: The presence of inverted Alu repeats within 3' UTRs causes nuclear retention.
source: For instance, the presence of inverted Alu repeats within 3' untranslated regions (3' UTRs) causes nuclear retention (Chen and Carmichael, 2009; Chen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated directly with supporting citations.

claim: Most Alu-exons will introduce a premature termination codon (PTC) into the transcript.
source: Moreover, most Alu-exons will introduce a premature termination codon (PTC) into the transcript, and Alu-exon transcripts are therefore likely to be targeted by nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD).
evidence: This is stated directly as a general characteristic of Alu-exons.

claim: The study identified 3101 new Alu-exons that are normally repressed by hnRNPC-mediated splicing repression and/or NMD-dependent mRNA surveillance in wild-type cells.
source: This identified 3101 new Alu-exons that are normally repressed by one or both pathways in wild-type cells.
evidence: This is stated as a key finding of the study.

claim: Upon hnRNPC but not UPF1 depletion, many Alu-exons are included together with flanking intronic sequences.
source: Upon hnRNPC but not UPF1 depletion, many Alu-exons are included together with flanking intronic sequences.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study.

claim: Intron-retaining Alu transcripts are generally resistant to NMD, even though they harbour PTCs, are exported to the cytoplasm and found in association with polysomes.
source: Surprisingly, these intron-retaining Alu transcripts are generally resistant to NMD, even though they harbour PTCs, are exported to the cytoplasm and found in association with polysomes.
evidence: This is stated as a surprising finding from the study.

claim: Evolutionary emergence of a stronger 3' splice site in an exonising Alu element is coupled with a longer repressive U-tract.
source: Analysing the evolutionary paths towards exonisation, we find that evolutionary emergence of a stronger 3' splice site in an exonising Alu element is coupled with a longer repressive U-tract.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from evolutionary analysis.

claim: Splicing repression by hnRNPC is decreased at ancient Alu elements, while they remain sensitive to NMD.
source: At the same time, splicing repression by hnRNPC is decreased at ancient Alu elements, while they remain sensitive to NMD.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study.

claim: Alu-exon formation proceeds through distinct evolutionary stages that rely on complementary repressive mechanisms.
source: We conclude that Alu-exon formation proceeds through distinct evolutionary stages that rely on complementary repressive mechanisms.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study.

claim: In the UCSC gene annotation, 2,657 Alu-exons are present (human genome version GRCh37/hg19).
source: In the UCSC gene annotation, 2,657 Alu-exons are present (human genome version GRCh37/hg19), for which at least one of the splice sites originates from an Alu element.
evidence: This is stated directly as a count from the UCSC annotation.

claim: Alu elements constitute 12.2% of the intronic sequence of protein-coding genes.
source: However, this is a relatively small number, given that Alu elements constitute 12.2% of the intronic sequence of protein-coding genes.
evidence: This is stated directly as a percentage.

claim: Only 4% of exonic sequence derives from Alu elements.
source: In contrast, only 4% of exonic sequence derives from Alu elements.
evidence: This is stated directly as a percentage.

claim: The contribution of Alu element sequences is less than 0.6% in constitutive exons.
source: Notably, the contribution of Alu element sequences is less than 0.6% in constitutive exons, indicating a strong bias towards alternative inclusion of Alu-exons.
evidence: This is stated directly as a percentage.

claim: There is a strong bias towards alternative inclusion of Alu-exons.
source: Notably, the contribution of Alu element sequences is less than 0.6% in constitutive exons, indicating a strong bias towards alternative inclusion of Alu-exons.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the low percentage in constitutive exons.

claim: The formation of alternative and constitutive Alu-exons is under tight control.
source: This suggests that the formation of alternative and constitutive Alu-exons is under tight control.
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion based on the bias towards alternative inclusion.

claim: A set of 4293 known Alu-exons was compiled, including 574 constitutive, 2083 alternative, and 1636 cryptic Alu-exons.
source: To characterise whether Alu-exons have an impact on gene expression, we compiled a set of 4293 known Alu-exons, including 574 and 2083 annotated as constitutive and alternative exons, respectively, as well as 1636 cryptic Alu-exons that we found in hnRNPC-depleted HeLa cells (Zarnack et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated directly as a description of the dataset compiled.

claim: In all tissues, Alu-exon genes with an alternative or a constitutive Alu-exon showed a clear trend to be less expressed than genes without Alu-exons.
source: In all tissues, Alu-exon genes with an alternative or a constitutive Alu-exon showed a clear trend to be less expressed than genes without Alu-exons, and this was most pronounced for genes containing a constitutive Alu-exon (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 1A.

claim: The reduced expression of Alu-exon genes is most pronounced for genes containing a constitutive Alu-exon.
source: In all tissues, Alu-exon genes with an alternative or a constitutive Alu-exon showed a clear trend to be less expressed than genes without Alu-exons, and this was most pronounced for genes containing a constitutive Alu-exon (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 1A.

claim: Only genes with cryptic Alu-exons showed a decrease in expression after hnRNPC depletion, while genes with annotated Alu-exons did not.
source: As predicted, only genes with cryptic Alu-exons showed a decrease in expression after hnRNPC depletion, while genes with annotated Alu-exons did not (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 1B.

claim: Cryptic Alu-exons were associated with decreased expression only in cytoplasmic but not nuclear RNA.
source: Moreover, cryptic Alu-exons were associated with decreased expression only in cytoplasmic but not nuclear RNA.
evidence: This is stated directly as a finding from the RNAseq data.

claim: qPCR validated the cytoplasmic loss of expression for nine out of nine well-expressed Alu-exon genes.
source: We used qPCR to validate the cytoplasmic loss of expression for nine out of nine well-expressed Alu-exon genes (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 1C.

claim: For two out of four genes (AGL, TIMM23), the Alu-exon transcripts were less abundant in the cytoplasm than in the nucleus.
source: For two out of four genes (AGL, TIMM23), the Alu-exon transcripts were less abundant in the cytoplasm than in the nucleus (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), and NUP133 showed more complex splicing patterns (see below).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The inclusion of Alu-exons followed by cytoplasmic loss of the Alu-exon transcripts frequently leads to reduced gene expression in response to hnRNPC depletion.
source: In summary, we conclude that the inclusion of Alu-exons followed by cytoplasmic loss of the Alu-exon transcripts frequently leads to reduced gene expression in response to hnRNPC depletion.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the data.

claim: No change in the cytoplasmic nor nuclear mRNA content was observed upon depletion of hnRNPC.
source: However, we did not observe any change in the cytoplasmic nor nuclear mRNA content upon depletion of hnRNPC (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: hnRNPC depletion did not change the kinetics of cytoplasmic mRNA accumulation of the ERK-induced genes FOS, ERG2 and NDRG1.
source: Within our time-course of 4-HT induction, hnRNPC depletion did not change the kinetics of cytoplasmic mRNA accumulation of the ERK-induced genes FOS, ERG2 and NDRG1 (Saito et al., 2013) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: The vast majority of Alu-exon and other genes did not show an expression pattern suggestive of an mRNA export block.
source: Moreover, the vast majority of Alu-exon and other genes did not show an expression pattern suggestive of an mRNA export block (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C), nor did we detect an increased nuclear accumulation of mature RNAs in dependence of hnRNPC (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 4C and 4D.

claim: The cytoplasmic loss of Alu-exon transcripts under hnRNPC knockdown conditions does not result from a nuclear export block, but instead might reflect their cytoplasmic degradation.
source: Hence, we observed neither a general nor an Alu-exon associated role of hnRNPC in mRNA export in our experiments. We therefore conclude that the cytoplasmic loss of Alu-exon transcripts under hnRNPC knockdown conditions in our study does not result from a nuclear export block, but instead might reflect their cytoplasmic degradation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the lack of evidence for export defects.

claim: NUP133 protein levels continue to decrease at later time points beyond the 48 hr of hnRNPC depletion.
source: We find that NUP133 protein levels continue to decrease at later time points beyond the 48 hr of hnRNPC depletion used in our experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 4E), which might cause the previously described mRNA export defects in hnRNPC-depleted cells (McCloskey et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 4E.

claim: Depletion of UPF1 led to up-regulation of known NMD targets.
source: As a control, we confirmed that UPF1 depletion led to up-regulation of known NMD targets (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B) and that among all exons detected in our RNAseq, PTC+ exons were significantly upregulated upon UPF1 depletion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Among all exons detected in the RNAseq, PTC+ exons were significantly upregulated upon UPF1 depletion.
source: As a control, we confirmed that UPF1 depletion led to up-regulation of known NMD targets (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B) and that among all exons detected in our RNAseq, PTC+ exons were significantly upregulated upon UPF1 depletion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Co-depletion of hnRNPC with UPF1 restores expression of Alu-exon genes caused by loss of hnRNPC.
source: Notably, co-depletion with UPF1 restores expression of Alu-exon genes caused by loss of hnRNPC (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 2A.

claim: NMD is involved in the cytoplasmic loss of Alu-exon transcripts.
source: This strongly suggests that NMD is involved in the cytoplasmic loss of Alu-exon transcripts and that hnRNPC-mediated splicing repression and NMD act together to repress Alu-exon expression.
evidence: This is stated as a strong suggestion based on the restoration of expression upon UPF1 depletion.

claim: hnRNPC-mediated splicing repression and NMD act together to repress Alu-exon expression.
source: This strongly suggests that NMD is involved in the cytoplasmic loss of Alu-exon transcripts and that hnRNPC-mediated splicing repression and NMD act together to repress Alu-exon expression.
evidence: This is stated as a strong suggestion based on the data.

claim: Depletion of either hnRNPC or UPF1 alone resulted in increased Alu-exon abundance and co-depletion of both factors showed a synergistic effect.
source: Indeed, changes in exon abundance analysed by DEXSeq (Anders et al., 2012) showed that depletion of either hnRNPC or UPF1 alone resulted in increased Alu-exon abundance and that co-depletion of both factors showed a synergistic effect (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 2B.

claim: The Alu-exons most strongly repressed by hnRNPC and UPF1 caused the most pronounced decrease in gene expression upon hnRNPC depletion.
source: The Alu-exons most strongly repressed by hnRNPC and UPF1 caused the most pronounced decrease in gene expression upon hnRNPC depletion, verifying a quantitative relationship between exon inclusion and reduced transcript abundance (Spearman rank correlation, p-value < 2.2e-16).
evidence: This is stated directly with statistical support.

claim: 746 of all Alu-exons are significantly repressed by either hnRNPC or UPF1.
source: In total, 746 of all Alu-exons are significantly repressed by either hnRNPC or UPF1 (adjusted p-value < 0.01).
evidence: This is stated directly as a count from the analysis.

claim: Approximately two-thirds of all hnRNPC-sensitive Alu-exons are refractory to NMD.
source: Intriguingly, approximately two-thirds of all hnRNPC-sensitive Alu-exons (hnRNPC-specific and shared-target) are refractory to NMD (Figure 2D), compared to one-third of alternative 'non-Alu' exons.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 2D.

claim: Almost 85% of the shared-target Alu-exons are within the CDS.
source: Almost 85% of the shared-target Alu-exons are within the CDS, compared to only 35% of the non-regulated Alu-exons, suggesting that repression of Alu-exons is particularly important within the CDS.
evidence: This is stated directly as a percentage from the analysis.

claim: Of 175 shared-target Alu-exons within the CDS, 65% introduce a PTC and additional 21% a frame-shift.
source: Of 175 shared-target Alu-exons within the CDS, 65% introduce a PTC and additional 21% a frame-shift, underlining their potentially deleterious impact.
evidence: This is stated directly as percentages from the analysis.

claim: ~40% of Alu-exon PTC+ isoforms are NMD-sensitive.
source: Given that ~40% of Alu-exon PTC+ isoforms are NMD-sensitive, Alu-exons are more efficient in eliciting NMD compared to other exons.
evidence: This is stated directly as a percentage from the analysis.

claim: Alu-exons are more efficient in eliciting NMD compared to other exons.
source: Given that ~40% of Alu-exon PTC+ isoforms are NMD-sensitive, Alu-exons are more efficient in eliciting NMD compared to other exons.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the comparison with other exons.

claim: Efficient NMD in mammalian cells requires the PTC to be at a distance of at least 55 nucleotides from the downstream exon-exon junction(s).
source: It was previously discovered that efficient NMD in mammalian cells requires the PTC to be at a distance of at least 55 nucleotides (nt) from the downstream exon-exon junction(s) in order to allow the exon junction complex (EJC) to recruit UPF1 (Le Hir et al., 2000; Nagy and Maquat, 1998; Thermann et al., 1998; Kervestin and Jacobson, 2012).
evidence: This is stated directly with supporting citations.

claim: PTCs are more frequently located less than 55 nt from the next exon-exon junction in NMD-refractory than in NMD-sensitive exons.
source: In line with the 55-nt rule, we found that in Alu-exons and all other types of alternative exons, PTCs are more frequently located less than 55 nt from the next exon-exon junction in NMD-refractory than in NMD-sensitive exons (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 2F.

claim: Only one-third of the NMD-refractory Alu-exons can be explained by a short distance of the PTC to the next exon-exon junction.
source: Nevertheless, only one-third of the NMD-refractory Alu-exons can be explained by a short distance of the PTC to the next exon-exon junction.
evidence: This is stated directly as a proportion from the analysis.

claim: Alu-exons are coordinately regulated by both splicing repression and NMD.
source: In summary, we found that Alu-exons are coordinately regulated by both splicing repression and NMD.
evidence: This is stated as a summary conclusion from the data.

claim: NMD accounts for the diminished expression of Alu-exon genes in hnRNPC-depleted cells.
source: While NMD accounts for the diminished expression of Alu-exon genes in hnRNPC-depleted cells, a substantial number of PTC+ Alu-exons is not cleared by the NMD pathway.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the data.

claim: A substantial number of PTC+ Alu-exons is not cleared by the NMD pathway.
source: While NMD accounts for the diminished expression of Alu-exon genes in hnRNPC-depleted cells, a substantial number of PTC+ Alu-exons is not cleared by the NMD pathway.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the data.

claim: Two-third of NMD-refractory Alu-exons cannot be explained by the 55-nt rule.
source: Notably, two-third of these NMD-refractory Alu-exons cannot be explained by the 55-nt rule, suggesting that additional mechanisms might be involved in controlling NMD sensitivity.
evidence: This is stated directly as a proportion from the analysis.

claim: Intron retention was found upstream or downstream of an Alu-exon for ~10% of Alu-exons in at least one of the tested conditions.
source: Using a modified DEXSeq approach to monitor intron events, we found retention of introns upstream or downstream of an Alu-exon for ~10% of Alu-exons in at least one of the tested conditions, including 40 cases of significant retention of both introns (adjusted p-value < 0.01; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The Alu-exons in intron-retaining Alu transcripts have weaker 5' and 3' splice sites.
source: The Alu-exons in these intron-retaining Alu transcripts have weaker 5' and 3' splice sites (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), indicating that intron retention might be a by-product of inefficient Alu exonisation.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Introns flanking potential Alu-exons were three to four times more frequently retained in hnRNPC-depleted cells compared to introns not containing an Alu-exon.
source: Compared to introns not containing an Alu-exon, introns flanking potential Alu-exons were three to four times more frequently retained in hnRNPC-depleted cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Intron retention in hnRNPC-depleted cells is significantly associated with Alu-exons.
source: Hence, intron retention in hnRNPC-depleted cells is significantly associated with Alu-exons.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the frequency of retention.

claim: No increased intron retention around repressed Alu-exons was observed in UPF1-depleted samples.
source: We did not observed increased intron retention around repressed Alu-exons in UPF1-depleted samples (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 3A.

claim: The intron-retaining Alu transcripts of NUP133 and MCM3 are readily detectable in cytoplasmic RNA.
source: However, we found that the intron-retaining Alu transcripts of NUP133 and MCM3 are readily detectable in cytoplasmic RNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Only the introns flanking the Alu-exon, but no other introns of the same transcripts are found in the cytoplasm.
source: Only the introns flanking the Alu-exon, but no other introns of the same transcripts are found in the cytoplasm (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 3B.

claim: No evidence for reduced nuclear export of intron-retaining Alu transcripts was found.
source: We did not observe accumulation of unspliced RNA in the nucleus for genes with intron-retaining Alu transcripts (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D), and thus, we found no evidence for reduced nuclear export of those transcripts.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 4D.

claim: The abundance of intron-retaining Alu transcripts was unchanged in UPF1-depleted cells.
source: Intriguingly, the abundance of intron-retaining Alu transcripts was unchanged in UPF1-depleted cells, suggesting that they are resistant to NMD (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 3C.

claim: The intron-retaining Alu transcripts of NUP133 as well as the NMD-refractory Alu-exon transcripts of TNPO3 and ZFX are present in the polysome fractions.
source: Semi-quantitative RT-PCR demonstrated that the intron-retaining Alu transcripts of NUP133 as well as the NMD-refractory Alu-exon transcripts of TNPO3 and ZFX are present in the polysome fractions, indicating that they might be translated (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 3D.

claim: Inclusion of intronic sequences flanking Alu-exons protects the resulting transcripts from NMD.
source: In summary, our data indicate that inclusion of intronic sequences flanking Alu-exons protects the resulting transcripts from NMD.
evidence: This is stated as a summary conclusion from the data.

claim: Exonising Alu elements have considerably stronger splice sites than other intronic Alu elements that do not give rise to Alu-exons.
source: Consistently, we found that exonising Alu elements have considerably stronger splice sites than other intronic Alu elements that do not give rise to Alu-exons (referred to as 'silent Alu elements'; Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 4A.

claim: Exonising Alu elements have longer U-tracts than silent Alu elements (median length of 11 nt compared to 7 nt).
source: Yet, exonising Alu elements have longer U-tracts than silent Alu elements (median length of 11 nt compared to 7 nt, Figure 4A and Zarnack et al., 2013), possibly suggesting a selection pressure for efficient hnRNPC repression.
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 4A.

claim: Mutations in the splice site sequences usually occur significantly after integration of the Alu element.
source: Previous phylogenetic maps across primate species showed that mutations in the splice site sequences usually occur significantly after integration of the Alu element (Krull et al., 2005; Singer et al., 2004), which would allow time for the U-tracts of the Alu-exon to decay through genomic drift.
evidence: This is stated directly with supporting citations.

claim: With increased sequence divergence, 3' splice site strength increases, while 5' splice site strength shows little variability.
source: With increased sequence divergence, 3' splice site strength increases, while 5' splice site strength shows little variability (Figure 4A, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 4A.

claim: In the oldest Alu-exons, the optimised 3' splice sites are accompanied by shorter U-tracts.
source: In the oldest Alu-exons, the optimised 3' splice sites are accompanied by shorter U-tracts (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), which leads to reduced repression by hnRNPC (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: Around half of emerging Alu-exons introduce a PTC or frame-shift irrespective of the divergence of the underlying Alu element.
source: In contrast, emerging Alu-exons do not seem to be under selective pressure to escape NMD, since around half of them introduce a PTC or frame-shift irrespective of the divergence of the underlying Alu element (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Alu-exons eventually escape strong hnRNPC repression by accumulating mutations that shorten their U-tracts.
source: Together, this indicated that Alu-exons eventually escape strong hnRNPC repression by accumulating mutations that shorten their U-tracts.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the evolutionary analysis.

claim: Alu-exon age and 3' splice site strength weakly correlated with maximum inclusion levels (Spearman's correlation coefficient ρ = 0.09 and ρ = 0.1, both p-values < 0.05).
source: Alu-exon age and 3' splice site strength weakly correlated with maximum inclusion levels (Spearman's correlation coefficient ρ = 0.09 and ρ = 0.1, both p-values < 0.05).
evidence: This is stated directly with statistical support.

claim: With increasing age, Alu-exons tend to be more frequently alternatively spliced between tissues.
source: With increasing age, Alu-exons tend to be more frequently alternatively spliced between tissues (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 4D.

claim: With increased age, Alu-exons tend to transition towards both higher and more tissue-specific inclusion.
source: Hence, we conclude that with increased age, Alu-exons tend to transition towards both higher and more tissue-specific inclusion.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the GTEx analysis.

claim: The Alu-exons with a cryptic 3' splice site early in evolution had shorter U-tracts compared to those where it emerged later.
source: The Alu-exons with a cryptic 3' splice site early in evolution had shorter U-tracts compared to those where it emerged later.
evidence: This is stated directly as a finding from the cross-species analysis.

claim: Emerging exons have longer U-tracts as evolution proceeds towards the human lineage, coupled with their increasing 3' splice site strength.
source: Strikingly, emerging exons have longer U-tracts as evolution proceeds towards the human lineage, coupled with their increasing 3' splice site strength, and the same trend is observed for evolving exons (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 5A and B.

claim: The U-tract is a crucial regulatory element in Alu elements, which is a target of selection during Alu exonisation, specifically at the stage of 3' splice site optimisation.
source: Overall, our intra- and inter-species analyses suggest that the U-tract is a crucial regulatory element in Alu elements, which is a target of selection during Alu exonisation, specifically at the stage of 3' splice site optimisation (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the evolutionary analyses.

claim: Long U-tracts couple the emerging 3' splice site with increasing splicing repression by hnRNPC, thus ensuring that most Alu-exons remain in a cryptic state.
source: Long U-tracts couple the emerging 3' splice site with increasing splicing repression by hnRNPC, thus ensuring that most Alu-exons remain in a cryptic state.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the data.

claim: U-tract length and repression by hnRNPC decline with increasing evolutionary age of the Alu element, despite the remaining presence of the strong 3' splice site.
source: Yet, U-tract length and repression by hnRNPC decline with increasing evolutionary age of the Alu element, despite the remaining presence of the strong 3' splice site.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the evolutionary analysis.

claim: Splicing repression by hnRNPC gradually decreases and Alu-exons escape splicing repression at a late stage of their evolution.
source: This demonstrates that splicing repression by hnRNPC gradually decreases and predicts that Alu-exons escape splicing repression at a late stage of their evolution.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion and prediction based on the data.

claim: Depletion of hnRNPC triggers the exonisation of hundreds of Alu elements.
source: Depletion of hnRNPC triggers the exonisation of hundreds of Alu elements (Zarnack et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated directly with a supporting citation.

claim: Depletion of UPF1 leads to a striking increase in the abundance of Alu-exons repressed by hnRNPC.
source: Here, we show that depletion of UPF1 leads to a striking increase in the abundance of Alu-exons repressed by hnRNPC, demonstrating that Alu-exon transcripts are substrates to the NMD pathway.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study.

claim: More than half of the Alu-exons are repressed by only one of the two pathways (hnRNPC or NMD).
source: Since more than half of the Alu-exons are repressed by only one of the two pathways, we predict that splicing repression and NMD are needed to safeguard gene expression from Alu-exonisation.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the data.

claim: Splicing repression and NMD are needed to safeguard gene expression from Alu-exonisation.
source: Since more than half of the Alu-exons are repressed by only one of the two pathways, we predict that splicing repression and NMD are needed to safeguard gene expression from Alu-exonisation.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction based on the data.

claim: Efficiency of NMD is decreased during differentiation of stem cells into neuronal precursors.
source: Physiologically, NMD itself is subjected to regulation under a variety of conditions; for example, efficiency of NMD is decreased during differentiation of stem cells into neuronal precursors (Lou et al., 2014) and in response to stress conditions, such as hypoxia, nutrient deprivation and infection (Fatscher et al., 2015; Hug et al., 2016; Gardner, 2008).
evidence: This is stated directly with supporting citations.

claim: Many transcripts that are normally degraded by NMD become upregulated under conditions where NMD efficiency is decreased.
source: As a result, many transcripts that are normally degraded by NMD become upregulated under these conditions (Gardner, 2008; Lou et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated directly with supporting citations.

claim: Alu-exons could have shaped the primate- and species-specific regulation of mRNA decay in response to variable efficiency of NMD.
source: Since we observed that many Alu-exons promote NMD, we speculate that Alu-exons could have shaped the primate- and species-specific regulation of mRNA decay in response to variable efficiency of NMD.
evidence: This is stated as speculation based on the findings.

claim: Most exonising Alu elements have not yet evolved to evade NMD.
source: This suggests that most exonising Alu elements have not yet evolved to evade NMD.
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion based on the persistence of PTCs.

claim: The Alu-derived alternative exon 10 in the gene CD55 is NMD-sensitive and causes a frame-shift, thereby generating a secreted CD55 protein isoform that is required for regulation of the complement cascade.
source: While speculative, the later explanation has precedence: The Alu-derived alternative exon 10 in the gene CD55 is NMD-sensitive (our study) and causes a frame-shift, thereby generating a secreted CD55 protein isoform that is required for regulation of the complement cascade (Osuka et al., 2006; Caras et al., 1987).
evidence: This is stated directly with supporting citations and data from the study.

claim: Even though the vast majority of Alu-containing transcripts contain PTCs, only about 40% are efficiently degraded by NMD.
source: Even though the vast majority of Alu-containing transcripts contain PTCs, only about 40% are efficiently degraded by NMD.
evidence: This is stated directly as a finding from the study.

claim: Only ~8% of annotated exons with a PTC undergo detectable NMD.
source: Yet, only ~8% of annotated exons with a PTC undergo detectable NMD (our study and McIlwain et al., 2010), suggesting that other exons with PTCs are more efficient in evading NMD than cryptic Alu-exons.
evidence: This is stated directly with supporting citations and data from the study.

claim: A PTC further than 55 nt from a downstream EJC is not sufficient to reliably predict NMD substrates.
source: Our analyses confirm previous findings that a PTC further than 55 nt from a downstream EJC is not sufficient to reliably predict NMD substrates (McIlwain et al., 2010; Lindeboom et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a confirmation of previous findings with supporting citations.

claim: Over 300 transcripts were found in which intronic sequences flanking an Alu-exon are retained.
source: A major finding of our study are over 300 transcripts, in which intronic sequences flanking an Alu-exon are retained.
evidence: This is stated as a major finding from the study.

claim: Intron-retaining Alu transcripts evade recognition by NMD despite the fact that they accumulate in the cytoplasm.
source: These intron-retaining Alu transcripts evade recognition by NMD despite the fact that they accumulate in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study.

claim: Past studies found that intron retention usually triggers either nuclear retention or NMD.
source: This is unexpected since past studies found that intron retention usually triggers either nuclear retention or NMD, separate mechanisms that are also exploited for specific regulation, e.g. to downregulate genes during cellular differentiation (Yap et al., 2012; Braunschweig et al., 2014; Wong et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated directly with supporting citations.

claim: NMD-resistant Alu-exon transcripts of TNPO3 and ZFX as well as the intron-retaining Alu transcript of NUP133 are associated with polysomes in a similar ratio as the conventionally spliced transcripts.
source: We observed that NMD-resistant Alu-exon transcripts of TNPO3 and ZFX as well as the intron-retaining Alu transcript of NUP133 are associated with polysomes in a similar ratio as the conventionally spliced transcripts.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study.

claim: The retained intronic sequences are usually longer than regular exons, likely resulting in an increased distance between any PTC and the next EJC.
source: Firstly, the retained intronic sequences are usually longer than regular exons, likely resulting in an increased distance between any PTC and the next EJC.
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation for NMD resistance.

claim: Splicing factors could remain bound on the retained introns and may prevent EJC assembly.
source: Secondly, splicing factors could remain bound on the retained introns and may prevent EJC assembly.
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation for NMD resistance.

claim: The retained introns may contain NMD-inhibitory sequences.
source: Thirdly, it is tempting to speculate that the retained introns may contain NMD-inhibitory sequences.
evidence: This is stated as speculation.

claim: A recent study described NMD-inhibitory, AU-rich sequences in some 3' UTRs, which are sufficient to block NMD in heterologous reporters.
source: A recent study described NMD-inhibitory, AU-rich sequences in some 3' UTRs, which are sufficient to block NMD in heterologous reporters (Toma et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated directly with a supporting citation.

claim: Introns generally show a higher A/U content than exonic sequences or Alu elements.
source: Since introns generally show a higher A/U content than exonic sequences or Alu elements (Amit et al., 2012; Louie et al., 2003), AU-rich or other sequence elements in the intron-retaining Alu transcripts may allow them to evade NMD.
evidence: This is stated directly with supporting citations.

claim: Intra- and inter-species analyses reveal longest U-tracts at Alu elements that recently acquired a 3' splice site.
source: Our intra- and inter-species analyses reveal longest U-tracts at Alu elements that recently acquired a 3' splice site, suggesting strongest selection pressure for repressive U-tracts during the initial evolutionary phase of cryptic Alu-exons (summarised in Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the evolutionary analyses.

claim: Alu-exons with stable 3' splice site across primate species show an average U-tract length of 8–10 uridines.
source: Interestingly, Alu-exons with stable 3' splice site across primate species show an average U-tract length of 8–10 uridines (Figure 5A and B), which is at the lower limit of 9 to 10 uridines necessary to allow cooperative binding by the two RRMs of hnRNPC (Cieniková et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 5A and B.

claim: A cryptic 3' splice site is best tolerated within an Alu element that already contains a long U-tract, while emergence of the same site in the absence of a long U-tract is subject to negative selection.
source: We propose that a cryptic 3' splice site is best tolerated within an Alu element that already contains a long U-tract, while emergence of the same site in the absence of a long U-tract is subject to negative selection.
evidence: This is stated as a proposal based on the data.

claim: Low inclusion of newly emerging exons is required to reduce negative selection against them.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, it was proposed that low inclusion of newly emerging exons is required to reduce negative selection against them (Xing and Lee, 2006).
evidence: This is stated as consistent with a previous proposal with a supporting citation.

claim: Long U-tracts are selected as balancing elements at splice sites increasing in strength due to random genomic drift.
source: While we cannot fully distinguish between scenarios of negative and positive selection, it is clear that long U-tracts are selected as balancing elements at splice sites increasing in strength due to random genomic drift.
evidence: This is stated as a clear conclusion from the data.

claim: Repression by the hnRNPC:U-tract interaction prevents abrupt increases in Alu-exon inclusion at strengthening 3' splice sites.
source: Repression by the hnRNPC:U-tract interaction prevents abrupt increases in Alu-exon inclusion at strengthening 3' splice sites, which could otherwise disrupt gene expression due to NMD or produce toxic proteins.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about the function of hnRNPC repression.

claim: Positive and negative splice sequences co-evolve at Alu-exons.
source: The selection pressure for long U-tracts favours Alu-exons with repressive elements in proximity to positive elements; effectively, positive and negative splice sequences co-evolve (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the evolutionary analysis.

claim: Regulatory co-evolution takes place while the Alu-exons are still in a cryptic state, before they acquire any functions.
source: Notably, this 'regulatory co-evolution' takes place while the Alu-exons are still in a cryptic state, before they acquire any functions.
evidence: This is stated as a notable observation from the data.

claim: Regulatory co-evolution may act to ensure a more gradual evolutionary path at emerging exons in general, and represent a crucial step in the emergence of new splice site sequences.
source: Regulatory co-evolution may act to ensure a more gradual evolutionary path at emerging exons in general, and represent a crucial step in the emergence of new splice site sequences.
evidence: This is stated as a possible general principle.

claim: Co-evolution of positive and negative splice elements has already been described at a set of constitutively included exons.
source: Co-evolution of positive and negative splice elements has already been described at a set of constitutively included exons (Xiao et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated directly with a supporting citation.

claim: Intronic G-tracts attract hnRNPH at 5' splice sites to enhance exons with intermediate-strength 5' splice sites.
source: Burge and colleagues proposed that intronic G-tracts attract hnRNPH at 5' splice sites to enhance exons with intermediate-strength 5' splice sites, and thus act as 'genetic buffers' at constitutive exons with mutations that weaken the 5' splice site sequence.
evidence: This is stated as a proposal from Burge and colleagues.

claim: Regulatory co-evolution describes a dynamic process in which evolving splice sites sequences are coupled to regulatory RBP binding sites, in order to maintain a stable level of exon recognition.
source: This illustrates that regulatory co-evolution describes a dynamic process in which evolving splice sites sequences are coupled to regulatory RBP binding sites, in order to maintain a stable level of exon recognition.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle illustrated by the examples.

claim: Regulatory co-evolution can either maintain exons in a cryptic state (in the case of U-tracts at Alu-exons), or in a constitutive state (in the case of G-tracts).
source: This process can thus either maintain exons in a cryptic state (in the case of U-tracts at Alu-exons), or in a constitutive state (in the case of G-tracts).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about the outcomes of regulatory co-evolution.

claim: Regulatory co-evolution opens an opportunity for evolutionary tinkering of the exon's sequence.
source: We propose that regulatory co-evolution opens an opportunity for evolutionary tinkering of the exon's sequence (Feschotte, 2008; Jacob, 1977; Sibley et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a proposal with supporting citations.

claim: While repressed through its U-tract, a cryptic exon might acquire mutations that decrease its toxicity, thus gradually decreasing the selection pressure for the repressive elements.
source: While repressed through its U-tract, a cryptic exon might acquire mutations that decrease its toxicity, thus gradually decreasing the selection pressure for the repressive elements.
evidence: This is stated as a possible scenario.

claim: If new sequence elements recruit repressors other than hnRNPC, which are not ubiquitously expressed, they could establish tissue-specific regulation of individual exons.
source: If new sequence elements recruit repressors other than hnRNPC, which are not ubiquitously expressed, they could establish tissue-specific regulation of individual exons.
evidence: This is stated as a possible scenario.

claim: Both an increase in maximum inclusion of an Alu-exon with increased Alu-exon age, and a trend towards a switch-like inclusion in individual tissues were observed.
source: We favour this scenario, since we observed both an increase in maximum inclusion of an Alu-exon with increased Alu-exon age, and a trend towards a switch-like inclusion in individual tissues.
evidence: This is stated as an observation supporting the favored scenario.

claim: The model of regulatory co-evolution of splice site sequences and RBP binding sites suggests that this process allows cells to maintain a delicate balance at newly emerging exons.
source: Our model of regulatory co-evolution of splice site sequences and RBP binding sites suggests that this process allows cells to maintain a delicate balance at newly emerging exons.
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion from the model.

claim: Cryptic Alu-exons with strong splice sites are coupled to repressive binding sites of hnRNPC, which allows them to be tolerated and thus to accumulate within primate transcripts.
source: Cryptic Alu-exons with strong splice sites are coupled to repressive binding sites of hnRNPC, which allows them to be tolerated and thus to accumulate within primate transcripts.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the model.

claim: The large number of cryptic Alu-exons exposes them to germline or somatic mutations that could disrupt the repressive U-tracts, thus leading to inclusion of potentially deleterious exons.
source: However, the large number of these cryptic Alu-exons exposes them to germline or somatic mutations that could disrupt the repressive U-tracts, thus leading to inclusion of potentially deleterious exons.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the large number of cryptic Alu-exons.

claim: The cryptic Alu-exons reported in this study could be considered for interpretation of whole-genome sequencing studies that aim to discover new disease-causing mutations.
source: We therefore propose that the cryptic Alu-exons reported in our study could be considered for interpretation of whole-genome sequencing studies that aim to discover new disease-causing mutations.
evidence: This is stated as a proposal for future applications.

claim: HR1 cells are a stable derivative from HEK293 cells.
source: HR1 cells (Ewings et al., 2007) were a gift from Simon Cook (Babraham Institute, Cambridge) and are a stable derivative from HEK293 cells (ATCC Cat# CRL-1573, RRID:CVCL_0045).
evidence: This is stated directly in the methods section.

claim: In HR1 cells, a total of 5205 Alu-exons were identified, including 3101 that were not identified in the previous study in HeLa cells.
source: In HR1 cells, we identified a total of 5205 Alu-exons, including 3101 that were not identified in our previous study in HeLa cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Together with further Alu-exons that are annotated in UCSC but not expressed in either cell type, evidence was found for 6309 non-overlapping exonising Alu elements within 4243 human genes.
source: Together with further Alu-exons that are annotated in UCSC but not expressed in either cell type, we found evidence for 6309 non-overlapping exonising Alu elements within 4243 human genes.
evidence: This is stated directly as a total count.

claim: 72 NMD-specific Alu-exons (hnRNPC-/NMD+) represent 10% of the significantly regulated Alu-exons.
source: This enabled us to classify the 746 significantly repressed Alu-exons as 'sensitive' or 'refractory' to either factor, resulting in three groups of exons (Figure 2D): 72 NMD-specific Alu-exons (hnRNPC-/NMD+, 10% of the significantly regulated Alu-exons), 465 hnRNPC-specific Alu-exons (hnRNPC+/NMD-, 62%), and 207 shared-target Alu-exons (hnRNPC+/NMD+, 28%).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 2D.

claim: 465 hnRNPC-specific Alu-exons (hnRNPC+/NMD-) represent 62% of the significantly regulated Alu-exons.
source: This enabled us to classify the 746 significantly repressed Alu-exons as 'sensitive' or 'refractory' to either factor, resulting in three groups of exons (Figure 2D): 72 NMD-specific Alu-exons (hnRNPC-/NMD+, 10% of the significantly regulated Alu-exons), 465 hnRNPC-specific Alu-exons (hnRNPC+/NMD-, 62%), and 207 shared-target Alu-exons (hnRNPC+/NMD+, 28%).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 2D.

claim: 207 shared-target Alu-exons (hnRNPC+/NMD+) represent 28% of the significantly regulated Alu-exons.
source: This enabled us to classify the 746 significantly repressed Alu-exons as 'sensitive' or 'refractory' to either factor, resulting in three groups of exons (Figure 2D): 72 NMD-specific Alu-exons (hnRNPC-/NMD+, 10% of the significantly regulated Alu-exons), 465 hnRNPC-specific Alu-exons (hnRNPC+/NMD-, 62%), and 207 shared-target Alu-exons (hnRNPC+/NMD+, 28%).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by Figure 2D.
